2.text: to last for the trade of the whole year. They have even bought wooden

3.text: storehouses brought on purpose from San Francisco.

4.text: At the present time the whole number of such storehouses on the Pacific

5.text: shore is fourteen. Indian Point has five, of which three belong to Kuvaˊr,

8.text: The whalers seldom skirt the Arctic coast westward from Uweˊlen, and

9.text: even then almost never go beyond Kuluˊči Bay. All the Maritime people
9.note: stress U+02CA after the second u, then č (c+U+030C, keying_spec.md §2.2) visibly caroned at 4x. Machine text read the stress mark as a slash ('Kulu/ci') and dropped the caron.

10.text: who wish to take part in this trading, resort, those from the Arctic villages,

11.text: to East Cape; those from the Pacific villages, to Indian Point. No positive

12.text: times are set for these gatherings; but, beginning with the middle of March,

13.text: the dog-teams and reindeer-caravans begin to appear one after another. They

14.text: keep coming long after the appearance of the first whaling-ships, because the

15.text: snow melts away only late in the spring. Travelling with skin boats begins

16.text: at the end of May, and from July on wholly replaces journeying with sledges.

17.text: Only skin boats are used, since it is difficult to make a landing with wooden

18.text: whaling-boats, owing to the heavy surf, and because they are too heavy to

20.text: Direct trading with the American natives has fallen off, because the whalers

21.text: act as middle-men. At the present time the American Eskimo have not enough

22.text: peltries and seal-skins to trade with the Asiatic natives, because all such things

23.text: go to the local white traders.

24.text: People from St. Lawrence and Diomede Islands often come over to the

25.text: Asiatic shore, for the most part on board the whalers, carrying their skin

26.text: boats with them for cases of emergency. Trading-parties from Indian Point

27.text: still go over in boats to St. Lawrence Island to barter reindeer-skins for spare

28.text: blubber, walrus-hides, and some whalebone, which last now forms an important

29.text: item in the native trade before it is sold to the whalers. They also gather

30.text: driftwood on the northern shore of the island, or buy roughly-hewn runners

31.text: and parts of skin-boat frames from the natives of the island. A similar trade

32.text: in wood and in roughly-hewn runners, dishes, trays, etc., is carried on across

33.text: Bering Strait. Enterprising men from Indian Point and East Cape sometimes

34.text: go over with the whalers to St. Michaels or to Cape Nome, carrying loads

35.text: of reindeer-skins, which are sold chiefly to the white people.
